findings.summary: contenttype.Parse accepts CR, LF, HTAB and NUL inside a quoted Content-Type parameter value, returning a parameter that upstream content-type rejects outright
findings.description:
## Summary

`github.com/malcolmston/express/contenttype`'s `Parse` used the pattern
`"(?:\\.|[^"\\])*"` for the quoted-string body of a Content-Type parameter. That
character class is "anything that is not a quote or a backslash", which admits
every control character: CR, LF, HTAB and NUL included.

The npm package this ports, `content-type@1.0.5`, restricts the quoted-string
body to `%x0b`, `%x20-21`, `%x23-5b`, `%x5d-7e` and obs-text `%x80-ff` (its
`PARAM_REGEXP`), and throws a `TypeError` for anything else. So where upstream
refuses to parse, the port succeeded and handed the caller a parameter value
containing the control bytes.

## Impact

A parameter value is routinely copied back out — into a response header, a log
line, a filename, a stored record. A value carrying `\r\n` is a header-splitting
primitive if it reaches a sink that does not re-validate; a value carrying NUL is
a truncation primitive in anything that later crosses into a C string. The port
was the component whose job it was to reject that input, and it did not.

Severity is **low** rather than high because the most common source of a
Content-Type value in a Go program is `net/http`, which rejects CR and LF in
inbound header values before a handler ever sees them, and because Go's own
`http.Header.Set` will not emit a header containing them. The exposure is real
but indirect: values that reach `Parse` from somewhere other than an
`http.Request` — a multipart part header, a database column, a config file, a
proxied upstream response body — were not filtered.

## Upstream vs port

```
input:  text/html; charset="utf-8\r\nX-Injected: 1"

content-type@1.0.5:  throws TypeError: invalid parameter format
port (<= 0.4.0):     ContentType{Type: "text/html",
                                  Parameters: {"charset": "utf-8\r\nX-Injected: 1"}}
```

## Repro

The finding was produced by the nested parity harness, which runs both
implementations over the same inputs:

```console
$ cd parity/express/nested/contenttype/node && npm install
$ cd .. && GOWORK=off go test .
--- FAIL: TestParity/p-quoted-with-crlf
    ok mismatch: upstream ok=false (invalid parameter format), go ok=true ()
```

The four case ids above are in [`cases/parse.json`](cases/parse.json).

## Fix

`Parse`'s parameter pattern now uses upstream's character class verbatim, and
`Format`'s output check uses upstream's `TEXT_REGEXP` (`%x0b`, `%x20-7e`,
`%x80-ff`) — the port previously allowed HTAB there and disallowed vertical tab,
which was wrong in both directions. Tabs are also no longer accepted as
parameter padding, matching upstream's spaces-only `; *name *= *value *`
grammar. All 76 parity cases now match. Regression vectors for the rejected
control characters were added to the package's `edge_test.go` and
`contenttype_parity_test.go`.
